Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) shares gained 5.96% to $169.94 as of 11:08 a.m. ET on Monday, November 9, in regular trading, as NPR reported that the company hired former Democratic Senator Jon Tester as an adviser. The move comes as Palantir expects closer congressional scrutiny of its government work, including immigration-enforcement contracts. Critics have accused the company of enabling surveillance; Palantir denies it collects data.

PLTR GF Value chart

The business itself is accelerating. Palantir reported third-quarter revenue of $2.31 billion, up 96% year over year. U.S. commercial revenue jumped 148% to $984 million, now ahead of U.S. government revenue of $953 million, which rose 96%. Adjusted operating margin reached 62%, and its Rule of 40 score hit 158%. Full-year revenue guidance rose to about $8.53 billion.

GuruFocus gives Palantir a GF Score of 85/100, with 10/10 Momentum, 9/10 Growth and 8/10 for Financial Strength and GF Value Rank. Profitability is the outlier at 4/10, suggesting the rank weighs a longer record than one quarter's 62% adjusted margin. The price sits about 23% below the GF Value of $220.53, yet the market value is roughly 48 times this year's guided revenue, so the model figure is no margin of safety. U.S. commercial revenue now exceeds government revenue, but government work still carries the reputational risk. The next test is whether congressional inquiries target specific contracts and whether U.S. commercial growth stays above 100%.

Key Takeaways

Palantir rose 5% today with no news of its own, as Cloudflare, Snowflake and other AI stocks rebounded from last week's selloff.

That selloff came after a quarter in which Palantir's revenue grew 96%.

ServiceNow and Adobe, both far cheaper AI software stocks, barely moved, so buyers went for the AI bets.

Palantir's drop went further than its business deserved, but its rich multiple will keep it swinging with the AI trade.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR:NASDAQ) is up 5% today, and there's no Palantir news behind it. Stocks are clawing back last week's AI-driven selloff.

Other AI names are bouncing too: Cloudflare (NET:NYSE) is up 10% and Snowflake (SNOW:NYSE) is up 6%. But cheaper AI software stocks like ServiceNow (NOW:NYSE) and Adobe (ADBE:NASDAQ) are close to flat.

Steve Eisman, the investor known for The Big Short, explained the slide on Friday's episode of The Real Eisman Playbook: "Palantir is a partial AI play and the market has been freaking out about all AI plays."

A big quarter, then a 10% drop

Palantir's third-quarter revenue rose 96% to $2.31 billion. But total contract value grew just 6%, and the stock fell. Then Democrats won both chambers of Congress, setting up a fight over the Pentagon's budget, and Palantir sank 10% on Thursday.

Analysts expect normalized EPS to more than double this year, to $1.70, and reach $3.73 by 2028.

The contract slowdown would have to show up in next year's revenue before analysts had much reason to cut those estimates.

The buyers went straight for AI

Cloudflare and Snowflake have growth of their own to point to. Cloudflare's third-quarter revenue, reported Thursday, rose 39%. Snowflake's product revenue grew 37% in the quarter ended July 31.

The cheaper names got left behind. ServiceNow is up just 1%, even though it raised its 2026 AI contract value target to $1.7 billion last month and traded at 23x forward earnings at Friday's close. Adobe is down 0.1% at 8.9x, even after its AI-first annual recurring revenue grew more than 150% in its latest quarter.

A Palantir office building in Tokyo_ Image by Hiroshi-Mori-Stock via Shutterstock_

Palantir (PLTR) just gave Wall Street a big surprise. In its most recent quarterly earnings report, U.S. commercial revenue topped U.S. government revenue for the first time in the company's history. Palantir's reliance on government revenue has been something the bulls have whined about for years. Now, though, Palantir is no longer only a defense contractor with a software side business. Its commercial engine has become a much larger feature.

During the third-quarter earnings call, CEO Alex Karp was fairly blunt. He noted how the commercial business had "eclipsed" Palantir's government business, moving from being a secondary growth area to a primary engine for the company. The impact of that is enormous, especially as the mix change should benefit Palantir's fortunes by de-risking and diversifying its business.

This is a structural change for the company. However, PLTR stock is still overvalued, and Wall Street isn't completely united in the belief that the U.S. commercial revenue news makes Palantir stock worth its current price. Let's take a closer look.

A Bumpy Ride for Palantir Stock

After soaring in 2025, Palantir stock has finally received a reality check this year, down 10% year-to-date (YTD). Shares hit a 52-week high of $212.94 in October 2026 but have cooled down since then.

The catalysts have been real. Sovereign AI deals with names like L3Harris (LHX) and Nvidia (NVDA) have lit a fire under Palantir stock. Goldman Sachs upgraded the stock to a "Buy" rating in early October with a $230 price target.

Still, the negatives are just as loud. Valuation fears keep capping every rally. Palantir stock fell after the Q3 earnings report despite a massive beat. Investors love the growth, but they hate the price.

Despite strong recent quarters, Palantir's valuation is considered extremely high, with a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio exceeding 118 times and an enterprise value-to-EBITDA multiple far above peers. That makes the stock vulnerable if growth slows or a market downturn occurs.

title: These 3 Stocks Just Fell After Strong Earnings. Here’s the One I’d Buy Right Now
detail:
These 3 Stocks Just Fell After Strong Earnings. Here’s the One I’d Buy Right Now
Matt Frankel, CFP®, The Motley Fool
Mon, November 9, 2026 at 8:11 AM CST 5 min read

PLTR
SHOP
NVDA

Trading disclosure

A good earnings report doesn't guarantee a stock will go up, and we've seen this many times throughout this earnings season. Last week, three widely held growth companies, Shopify (NASDAQ:SHOP), Datadog (NASDAQ:DDOG) and Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR), reported better-than-expected results, and all three stocks fell anyway.

In each case, the selling had less to do with the quarter that just ended and more to do with valuation or forward-looking guidance. Here's a rundown of what happened with each, what I think it means for investors, and which of the three I'd be comfortable buying right now.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

1. Shopify

Shopify grew its revenue by 32% to $3.74 billion in the third quarter, increased its operating income by 66%, and generated 22% of its revenue as free cash flow. Adjusted earnings of $0.49 per share beat the $0.47 consensus. The company also spent $562 million buying back its own stock, a vote of confidence from management that the stock is attractive.

The main problem was gross merchandise volume (GMV), the total value of sales on Shopify's platform. GMV grew 29% to $119.1 billion, slightly below estimates and slower than the 32% growth Shopify reported in the second quarter. As a result, the stock fell sharply on the day of the report.

I own Shopify, and I explained why I'm not planning to sell in a separate article. In short, a small GMV miss doesn't change my view of a business growing this fast while expanding its margins.

2. Datadog

Datadog, which sells software that helps companies monitor their cloud applications, grew revenue 35% to $1.2 billion. Adjusted earnings of $0.81 per share crushed the $0.64 consensus, and management raised its full-year revenue forecast.

Like several other AI-related stocks that recently fell after strong earnings, Datadog's main issue was guidance. Datadog expects fourth-quarter revenue of $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion, roughly flat with the third quarter, which is an unusual pause for a company growing this fast. Datadog had already warned that its largest customer would use less of its services starting in the third quarter, so this could be the main reason. But even so, the stock fell more than 14% the day after the report and is now about 40% below its recent high, reached in early October.

Prediction market operator Kalshi launched single-stock perpetual futures on Nov. 5 across more than 50 NYSE- and Nasdaq-listed names, claiming more than $300 million in volume within hours of a quiet launch, a figure that is self-reported rather than audited and that was dominated by SpaceX-linked contracts.

Perps tied to SpaceX (SPCX) led early trading at roughly $88 million in 24-hour volume, equal to nearly 30% of Kalshi's headline launch tally even though the two figures cover different windows, which shows that demand clusters around high-attention names.

The roster of single-stock perps also includes Palantir (PLTR), Meta (META), Nvidia (NVDA), and McDonald's (MCD), making the rollout the most direct challenge yet from the prediction-market cohort to the incumbent equity-derivatives establishment.

How Kalshi's Stock Perps Work

The structure of Kalshi's single-stock perpetual futures is retail-friendly by design, with each contract representing 0.02 shares, settling in cash, and staying tethered to the underlying stock through a daily 4:00 p.m. ET funding payment, which is the periodic transfer that keeps a never-expiring perpetual contract priced near the stock.

Leverage is capped near 5x, well below the 50x to 100x common offshore. That positions the product as a lower-octane, regulated cousin of crypto-style perps.

Micron's Plunge Set the Stage

The timing is notable because Micron (MU) fell 23% in two days after the midterm elections amid a broad AI-sector selloff, which is exactly the kind of volatility that draws leveraged speculators to frictionless shorting tools.

The CFTC cleared the products as security futures under joint CFTC and SEC oversight, and Kalshi is already filing with the SEC to shorten listing timelines for newly public companies.

That SEC filing signals Kalshi intends to push the product toward fresh listings quickly rather than wait for the legal fight to settle.

Futures or Swaps? Cboe and Citadel Securities Sue

An alliance that includes Cboe (CBOE) and Ken Griffin's Citadel Securities has sued, arguing that perps are functionally swaps rather than futures. The industry heavyweights claim that perpetual funding payments meet the Dodd-Frank definition of a swap, a classification that would trigger stricter margin, capital, and reporting rules and limit retail access.

title: Here is What to Know Beyond Why Palantir Technologies Inc. (PLTR) is a Trending Stock

Here is What to Know Beyond Why Palantir Technologies Inc. (PLTR) is a Trending Stock

Palantir Technologies Inc. (PLTR) has been one of the most searched-for stocks on Zacks.com lately. So, you might want to look at some of the facts that could shape the stock's performance in the near term.

Shares of this company have returned -23.3% over the past month versus the Zacks S&P 500 composite's -5.6% change. The Zacks Internet - Software industry, to which Palantir Technologies belongs, has lost 13.4% over this period. Now the key question is: Where could the stock be headed in the near term?

Although media reports or rumors about a significant change in a company's business prospects usually cause its stock to trend and lead to an immediate price change, there are always certain fundamental factors that ultimately drive the buy-and-hold decision.

Revisions to Earnings Estimates

Rather than focusing on anything else, we at Zacks prioritize evaluating the change in a company's earnings projection. This is because we believe the fair value for its stock is determined by the present value of its future stream of earnings.

We essentially look at how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to reflect the impact of the latest business trends. And if earnings estimates go up for a company, the fair value for its stock goes up. A higher fair value than the current market price drives investors' interest in buying the stock, leading to its price moving higher. This is why empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.

Palantir Technologies is expected to post earnings of $0.52 per share for the current quarter, representing a year-over-year change of +108%. Over the last 30 days, the Zacks Consensus Estimate has changed +6.5%.

For the current fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $1.7 points to a change of +126.7% from the prior year. Over the last 30 days, this estimate has changed +3.2%.

For the next fiscal year, the consensus earnings estimate of $2.49 indicates a change of +46.2% from what Palantir Technologies is expected to report a year ago. Over the past month, the estimate has changed +7.4%.

Having a strong externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, offers a more conclusive picture of a stock's price direction in the near term, since it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions. Due to the size of the recent change in the consensus estimate, along with three other factors related to earnings estimates, Palantir Technologies is rated Zacks Rank #3 (Hold).

For the better part of the last four years, no catalyst has played a bigger role in lifting the broader market than the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI). Whether it's AI-accelerating hardware or AI applications, an IDC report pegs this cumulative addressable opportunity at $22.5 trillion from 2025 to 2031.

Few companies have taken the AI bull by the horns more than Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR), and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs) are the infrastructure backbone of AI-accelerated data centers. None of its competitors are particularly close to matching the compute capabilities of its multiple generations of GPUs.

Meanwhile, AI-driven software-as-a-service provider Palantir is a veritable blueprint for deploying AI applications. The company's Gotham platform assists the U.S. military with planning and overseeing missions.

Electric-vehicle maker Tesla is also an AI applications maven. AI is integral to the success of its full self-driving software and its Optimus humanoid robots.

Image source: Getty Images.

While this trio has thrived amid the AI infrastructure build-out, the individuals who know these companies best are sending all the wrong signals to Wall Street.

Nvidia's, Palantir's, and Tesla's insiders are shaking Wall Street to its core

Though stock market analysts spend day after day studying the same industry and the companies that define it, no one understands Nvidia, Palantir, and Tesla better than their respective insiders.

An "insider" is a high-ranking executive, board member, or beneficial owner of at least 10% of a company's outstanding shares who may possess nonpublic information. Anytime an insider buys or sells their company's stock, they're legally required to file Form 4 with regulators within two business days. This allows investors to track whether a company's insiders have been buying or selling.

In the case of this powerhouse AI trio, insiders have been undeniable net sellers of their company's stock over the trailing five years:

Nvidia: $6,860,636,476 in net selling

Palantir: $6,371,606,538 in net selling

Tesla: $39,479,555,646 in net selling

Collectively, insiders at these companies have sold more than $52.7 billion more of their own company's stock than they've purchased since early November 2021.
